subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Qualitative research methods (interviews, observations, case studies)

questions.q: An experiment can establish cause and effect because the researcher:
options: Manipulates an independent variable and controls extraneous variables
Measures two variables as they naturally vary
questions.explain: Deliberate manipulation of the IV plus control of confounds allows changes in the DV to be attributed to the IV.

questions.q: In an experiment, the variable that the researcher deliberately changes is the:
questions.explain: The independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is measured to see the effect.

questions.q: A correlational study can show that two variables are related, but it cannot:
options: Establish that one variable causes the other
questions.explain: Correlation indicates association only; a third variable or reverse causation may explain the relationship.

questions.q: A study reports that as ice-cream sales rise, so do drowning rates. The best interpretation is that:
options: A third variable, such as hot weather, may drive both
The correlation must be an error
questions.explain: This classic example shows a confounding third variable can produce a correlation without any direct causal link.

questions.q: A directional (one-tailed) hypothesis differs from a non-directional one because it:
options: Predicts the direction of the difference or relationship
States that there will be no effect
Can only be used in interviews
questions.explain: A directional hypothesis specifies which way results will go, usually when previous research justifies the prediction.

questions.q: Randomly allocating participants to experimental conditions mainly helps to:
options: Distribute participant variables evenly and reduce bias
Remove the need for a hypothesis
questions.explain: Random allocation spreads individual differences across conditions, reducing systematic bias from participant variables.

questions.q: A positive correlation means that as one variable increases, the other:
questions.explain: In a positive correlation the two variables move in the same direction; in a negative correlation they move oppositely.

questions.q: Qualitative research methods are designed primarily to gather:
options: Rich, detailed, non-numerical data about meaning and experience
questions.explain: Qualitative methods explore how people understand and experience phenomena, producing in-depth textual data.

questions.q: A semi-structured interview is characterised by:
options: A set of core questions with freedom to follow up and explore responses
A fixed script that cannot be departed from
questions.explain: Semi-structured interviews balance consistency with flexibility, allowing the interviewer to probe interesting answers.

questions.q: A case study is best described as:
options: An in-depth investigation of a single individual, group or event
A large-scale experiment with random allocation
questions.explain: Case studies provide detailed, holistic data on one case, often using multiple methods.

questions.q: A strength of case studies is their rich detail, but a common limitation is that:
options: Findings from a single case are difficult to generalize
questions.explain: Because they focus on one case, results may not apply to the wider population, though they are valuable for rare phenomena.

questions.q: A researcher wants to understand how refugees experience resettlement in their own words. The most appropriate method is:
options: A correlational survey of income only
questions.explain: Understanding lived experience and meaning is best suited to qualitative interviewing rather than an experiment.

questions.q: In qualitative research, using several data sources or methods to check findings is called:
questions.explain: Triangulation strengthens the credibility (trustworthiness) of qualitative findings by cross-checking across sources or methods.

questions.q: In a random sample, every member of the target population has:
options: An equal chance of being selected
A chance based on how willing they are
To be chosen by the researcher personally
questions.explain: Random sampling gives each population member an equal probability of selection, improving representativeness.

questions.q: Opportunity sampling involves selecting participants who are:
questions.explain: Opportunity sampling uses whoever is accessible, which is practical but risks an unrepresentative sample.

questions.q: A limitation of opportunity and volunteer samples is that they:
options: May be unrepresentative and introduce bias
questions.explain: Such samples may over-represent particular types of people, limiting how far results generalize.

questions.q: Purposive sampling selects participants because they:
options: Have specific characteristics relevant to the research question
questions.explain: Purposive sampling deliberately targets people with the traits or experiences the study requires, common in qualitative work.

questions.q: A researcher recruits participants by placing an advertisement and using those who respond. This is:
questions.explain: Volunteers who respond to an advert form a self-selected sample, which can be biased towards certain motivations or traits.

questions.q: Compared with a small convenience sample, a larger and more representative sample generally improves:
options: The manipulation of the independent variable
questions.explain: More representative samples allow findings to be applied more confidently to the target population.

questions.q: Informed consent requires that participants:
options: Are given enough information about the study to agree freely
Never learn the aim of the study
questions.explain: Participants should understand what is involved and agree voluntarily before taking part.

questions.q: The use of deception in a study can be justified only when:
options: It is necessary, causes minimal harm, and participants are fully debriefed
questions.explain: Deception must be essential, kept to a minimum, and followed by a debrief that restores understanding and wellbeing.

questions.q: The right to withdraw means that participants:
options: May leave the study at any time and can withdraw their data
Must complete the study once started
Give up all rights on consenting
questions.explain: Participants can stop taking part at any point and, in many guidelines, request that their data be removed.

questions.q: Maintaining confidentiality and anonymity in research protects:
questions.explain: Keeping data confidential and anonymised safeguards participants from harm and respects their privacy.

questions.q: After running a memory study that involved a cover story, the researcher must:
options: Debrief participants, explaining the true aim and addressing any concerns
questions.explain: A full debrief is essential after deception to inform participants and check on their wellbeing.
